prompt: Server room workbench. An isometric cutaway of a GPU workstation: two M.2 consumer SSDs with copper heat spreaders sit in a drive cage at left; a central CPU socket with exposed processor cores and a small cooling tower; at right, a full-height accelerator card with dense aluminium fins and polymer shroud. A thin safety-yellow data ribbon runs from drives to CPU, then to the accelerator's PCIe slot, constricting sharply at the GPU input. Raking light from upper left across brushed steel and concrete. Palette graphite, cobalt, safety yellow. Extreme asymmetry: accelerator off-centre right, drives left. No text.

rationale: The article explains how a training feed actually works as a system, and an isometric cutaway can name each part — drives, cores, accelerator — while showing the constriction at the GPU. It states the mechanism physically instead of relying on a generic server rack.
subject: an isometric cutaway of a GPU workstation showing consumer SSDs, processor cores, and an accelerator with a constricting data ribbon
core_thesis: A training accelerator consumes 5.9 GiB/s of steady read, and the measured stall survives even a fully cached dataset, so the next purchase is processor cores, not a faster drive.
core_conflict: Storage throughput meets accelerator consumption at a fixed feed rate; capacity and feed are different purchases, and the stall upstream in the decode path decides whether the GPU is busy or starved.
composition: extreme asymmetry; accelerator card dominates right third, drives left, data ribbon pulls eye to GPU
